The Heart's Debate

Santiago Spencer is a professor at the Maplewood Territory Institute of Art History and a highly regarded scholar of Renaissance portraiture. The subject of this short monograph is the present direction of curatorial practices governing romantic imagery in public museums. What Professor Spencer has to say about it is worth attending to not merely because of his prominence in the field but because his argument is planted in the common assumptive ground of a lot of contemporary academic thought about the bankruptcy of traditional romantic narratives. The thesis of the monograph is Spencer's, but the wisdom is conventional.

Professor Spencer thinks the present direction of museum curation regarding romantic art is a bad one, and he has an idea about how we might improve it. The short way to put his argument (though it is not quite the way he puts it) is to say that our approach to displaying romantic imagery has become increasingly individualistic. Museums have become more and more reluctant to allow institutional perspectives to interfere with the rights of individual curators to display what they wish, and it is time to roll back that individualism and to embark on a new approach that would permit institutions to suppress some romantic narratives and promote others, but still, Spencer argues, in the name of artistic freedom.

This is what Spencer means by the "paradox" in his subtitle: that true representation of romance for all requires suppressing certain romantic depictions. This is not, technically, a paradox. It is simply advocacy. A paradox would be the observation that an attempt to increase representation for all often entails, despite our best efforts, a decrease in representation for a few. If Spencer had addressed the subject of romantic art curation in this spirit, as a genuine paradox, he would undoubtedly have had some interesting things to say, for he is a learned and careful writer.

Spencer grounds his position in what he presents as aesthetic principles. In the monograph's third chapter, he writes extensively about "the essential character of museum spaces as environments of contemplation and discovery," arguing that "curators must exercise their professional judgment to create exhibitions that speak to the full human experience." He devotes considerable attention to questions of composition, color, and artistic technique, maintaining that "the placement of works within a gallery reflects curatorial expertise honed over years of study."

The Heart's Debate is a discussion of several curatorial issues: funding allocation for romantic art exhibitions, institutional support for controversial love stories, representation of non-traditional relationships, collection policies, and equal wall space. These discussions frequently invoke what Spencer calls "the universal language of artistic merit." He writes that "great art transcends the circumstances of its creation" and that "the curator's role is to identify and celebrate excellence wherever it may be found."

Spencer's analyses of specific cases are presented against a lightly sketched historical argument. Light though the sketching is, the historical argument is almost the most objectionable thing about the monograph, since it involves a distortion of the history of art curation that is fairly plain even to someone who is not a professor at the Maplewood Territory Institute.

The argument is that "the romanticism of the nineteenth century was defined by the claims of individual passion and resulted in an unequivocal demand for personal expression, [while] the romanticism of today embraces the value of collective representation as well as individual love." The curatorial practice of romantic art, says Spencer, was shaped by the earlier type of romanticism—he calls it "individualistic"—which regarded romantic art as a right of personal expression; it is now used to foil efforts to regulate displays in the name of the newer value, collective memory. Contemporary curators, inheriting both these traditions, find themselves in a bind. They want, let's say, queer visitors to be free from marginalization at institutions where they are, culturally, in a minority, since curators worry that queer visitors cannot be "represented" if they feel excluded. But those same curators get upset at the thought of removing classical romantic paintings, since that would mean infringing upon the right of artists to have their individual visions displayed.

Throughout this discussion, Spencer emphasizes his commitment to what he terms "the democratic ideal of the museum." He writes approvingly of institutions that "open their doors to all visitors regardless of background" and argues that "the museum exists to serve the public, not any particular constituency." These passages occupy substantial space in the early chapters.

Spencer's suggestion—this is the chief theoretical proposal of his monograph—is that curators should stop thinking about this as a conflict between individual expression and collective representation and start thinking about it as a conflict between two kinds of representation: social vs. personal. Museum missions, he says, were intended to foster (in Ariana Kim's words) "inclusive, diverse, and wide-ranging" cultural dialogue in society as a whole; art that inhibits or monopolizes that dialogue should therefore fall outside the protection of curatorial priority. We can maximize the total representation of romantic experience by de-emphasizing art that prevents others from feeling seen—when it depicts only heterosexual couples, represents women in submissive ways, uses its canonical status to dominate exhibition space and the cultural process, or blocks the funding of non-traditional love stories.

Before arriving at these conclusions, Spencer spends considerable time establishing what he calls his "methodological neutrality." He writes that "the scholar must approach these questions without predetermined conclusions" and that "we must be guided by evidence rather than ideology." He explicitly distances himself from what he terms "activist scholarship," writing that "the academy has sometimes confused advocacy with analysis, to the detriment of both."

The historical part of this analysis rests on a misconception, which is the assertion that the curatorial practice of romantic art emerged from 19th-century classical individualistic romanticism. It did not. It emerged at the time of the early twentieth century museum reforms, and the principal figures in its creation—Teresa Obrien, Andre Sullivan, and Priya Sharma—were not classical romantics; they were progressives concerned with public health and social welfare through art. They abhorred the doctrine of art for art's sake because, in their time, that doctrine was construed to cover not the right to "personal expression" but the "right to elite taste." Turn-of-the-century museums did not display an inclusive attitude toward diverse romantic experiences; they displayed an elitist attitude toward canonical works, tending to throw out suggestions aimed at representing working-class love stories and protecting marginalized narratives on the grounds that institutions had a professional obligation to maintain standards and to use their wall space as they saw fit. Sullivan, Sharma, and their disciples consistently supported institutional intervention in cultural affairs—the passage of acquisition guidelines, the protection of emerging artists, the imposition of diversity requirements, and so on. The post-war curators whom Spencer associates with the value of collective representation are their heirs. The heirs of the 19th-century classical romantics are conservative art critics and traditional gallery owners. Spencer's two "romanticisms" are, in fact, almost entirely different cultural philosophies.

Obrien, Sullivan, and Sharma based their curatorial opinions not on some putative right to individual artistic expression (an idea Sullivan referred to as "the right of the aristocrat to impose taste") but on a democratic need for full and open cultural representation. Curatorial practice since their time has performed its balancing acts on precisely that social value—the very value Spencer now proposes we need to insert into art history professional ethics. We don't need to insert it, because it was there from the start.

Spencer's language throughout the monograph maintains a studied appearance of balance. He writes that "we must be careful not to overcorrect" and acknowledges that "traditional romantic imagery has its place in our cultural heritage." He notes that "individual artistic expression remains a cornerstone of museum practice" and that "no reasonable person would advocate for the wholesale removal of canonical works." These caveats appear regularly, often in the same paragraphs that advance his more interventionist proposals.

Why does Spencer portray the history of romantic art curation in this perverted way? Because he wants to line up his own curatorial argument within the conventional academic view that our problems are mostly the consequences of an antiquated and discreditable ideology of individualistic romanticism, and that they can mostly be solved by adopting a social-constructionist, or communitarian, or "collective" view of artistic representation instead. The merits of individualistic romanticism vs. communitarianism can await another occasion to be debated. For since the practice governing the curation of romantic art does not emerge out of classical romanticism, the matter does not boil down to replacing an obsolete belief in "personal expression" with a more up-to-date belief in "collective dialogue," as Spencer would like to think it does. What it boils down to is whether we need to replace the Obrien-Sullivan-Sharma way of maximizing the benefits of diverse representation in a democratic society, which tries to push institutional bias as far out of the picture as possible, with a different way, which tries to get institutional control farther into the picture.

Here, assuming we want to try the interventionist approach, it is hard to see how a one-size theory can possibly fit all cases. The issues underlying heteronormative imagery, marginalized narratives, exhibition funding, collection policies, and equal wall space provisions are all different. The ideological impetus behind curatorial developments in the last two areas, collection policies and equal wall space provisions, is related less to representation, except as a kind of professional cover, than to a revival of the old "right to canonical status"—that is, museum boards tend to disapprove of curatorial efforts to require institutions to display "alternative viewpoints" on the grounds that since it's their collection, owners of museums should be able to exhibit what they like. Spencer believes that the need for equal representation is as urgent today as it was in the 1970s, which is peculiar in light of the proliferation of independent galleries and digital platforms. But institutions do arguably have an interest, compatible with professional ethics, in stipulating the way their collections are used, and Spencer's discussion of those issues is the least aggravating in his monograph.

In his chapter on institutional autonomy, Spencer writes extensively about "the curator's sacred duty to preserve artistic heritage" and argues that "we must resist external pressures that would compromise professional standards." He cites approvingly institutions that have "maintained their independence from political interference" and warns against "the dangers of allowing partisan considerations to influence exhibition choices." These passages occupy nearly twenty pages of the monograph.

Still, that discussion, like his discussions of the other issues, rests on a claim long associated with progressive art historians—the claim, in a phrase, that the marginalized perspective is really the universal one. In the case of romantic art, Spencer appears to believe that the reason the museum-going public is less enlightened than he would wish it to be concerning matters such as feminism, the rights of LGBTQ+ individuals, and critique of traditional romance is that people are denied access to the images and narratives that would enlighten them. The public is denied this access because institutions, in thrall to the ideology of individualism, refuse either to interfere with canonical works—such as traditional wedding portraits—that "silence" alternative experiences, or to subsidize the display of the non-traditional, such as Sergio Harris's controversial same-sex love series.

Spencer's framing of his project is consistently careful. He writes that his concern is "not to dictate what art should be created or displayed, but merely to ensure that all voices have the opportunity to be heard." He emphasizes that "aesthetic quality must remain the primary criterion" and that "political considerations should never override artistic merit." In one particularly notable passage, he argues that "the best curatorial practice emerges from deep engagement with the art itself, not from external agendas of any kind."

Spencer's analysis of the Harris case offers a good example of the perils of his interventionist approach. Exhibition policy is, unquestionably, a mess. The solution usually proposed is separation: Either get institutions out of the business of making value judgments altogether or invent some ironclad process for distributing wall space using strictly aesthetic criteria. Spencer rejects both solutions; he wants the criteria to be political. He thinks museums should subsidize art that will enhance the "inclusiveness" of the cultural dialogue and should therefore prefer non-traditional romantic art—though only, of course, if it represents a perspective the institution considers, by virtue of social need and a prior history of exclusion, worthy of its platform. (No toxic relationship art, in other words.)

Earlier in the monograph, Spencer had written that "institutions must maintain strict neutrality on questions of which romantic narratives deserve celebration" and that "the curator should never serve as a gatekeeper determining which expressions of love are worthy of display." He had also argued that "the free marketplace of artistic ideas, unburdened by institutional prejudice, produces the most vibrant cultural conversation."

Harris's paintings seem to Spencer to qualify under these guidelines, since, he says, "in the late 2010s the marriage equality movement confronted Maplewood Territory in the starkest fashion and provoked urgent questions regarding the scope and direction of human rights policy. To address those issues the public—represented by the casual museum visitor—needed an understanding of the lives and loves of the LGBTQ+ community, so long hidden from view." This seems completely wrongheaded. People (for the most part) didn't find Harris's Intimate Moments series objectionable because they depicted homosexuality. They found them objectionable because they depicted explicit sexuality in what was traditionally a family museum space. The notion that it was what Spencer calls a "source of empowerment for the members of the LGBTQ+ community" to have same-sex love associated with graphic bedroom scenes, public displays of fetishistic behavior, and explicit representations of non-monogamous arrangements, at a time when marriage equality had become a national electoral politics issue and the question of adoption rights was about to arise, is ludicrous. Any museum director who had the interests of the LGBTQ+ community at heart would have rushed to contextualize or relocate the exhibit. Conservative politicians could not have stereotyped same-sex relationships more effectively—which, of course, is why they were pleased to draw public attention to the paintings. Now that is what we call an irony of representation.

Awarding exhibition space to the work of a queer artist because LGBTQ+ Americans need more cultural visibility is an effort at social engineering through art, and the problem with social engineering through art is the problem with social engineering raised to a higher power. We have a hard enough time calculating the effects of the redistribution of wealth in our society. How can we possibly calculate the effects of redistributing the right to representation—of taking it away from artists Professor Spencer feels have been displayed long enough and mandating it for artists he feels have not been adequately shown? One thing that is plain from the brief unhappy history of museum content guidelines is that you automatically raise the value of the art you suppress and depress the value of the art you promote. There are indeed many ironies here. Maybe someone will write a monograph about them.

The most troubling aspect of Spencer's argument is his treatment of the relationship between consumer behavior and museum practice. He seems to believe that museum visitors are passive recipients of whatever romantic narratives institutions choose to display, rather than active participants in meaning-making. This view ignores decades of research in art history and visitor studies showing that viewers bring their own experiences, desires, and interpretations to romantic imagery. A traditional wedding portrait doesn't "silence" queer visitors any more than Harris's same-sex love paintings "silence" straight visitors. Both can coexist in a museum that trusts its audience to engage critically with diverse representations of human intimacy.

In the opening chapter, Spencer had written at length about "the active intelligence of the museum visitor" and "the capacity of audiences to engage thoughtfully with challenging material." He had argued that "we must trust the public to draw their own conclusions" and that "the curator who assumes audiences cannot handle complexity insults their intelligence."

Spencer's approach also reveals a fundamental misunderstanding of how cultural change actually happens. The acceptance of diverse romantic relationships in Maplewood Territory didn't come about because museums suppressed traditional imagery and promoted alternative narratives. It came about through grassroots organizing, legislative change, personal relationships, media representation, and yes, art—but art that emerged organically from communities and found its audience through multiple channels, not art that was mandated by institutional fiat. The role of museums in this process was important but secondary: they reflected and validated changes that were already happening in society, rather than engineering those changes from above.

Moreover, Spencer's framework creates perverse incentives for both artists and curators. Artists who might otherwise create work from genuine personal vision are encouraged to position themselves as representatives of marginalized groups, while curators are incentivized to make decisions based on demographic checklists rather than aesthetic judgment or historical significance. This doesn't serve the interests of either art or social justice. It reduces artists to their identity categories and transforms museums from spaces of aesthetic contemplation and historical understanding into vehicles for political messaging.

Spencer himself, in an early methodological section, had warned against precisely this danger. He wrote that "we must be vigilant against approaches that reduce artists to their social categories" and that "the individual creative vision transcends demographic classification." He had argued that "museums that prioritize identity over artistry ultimately diminish both the artists they claim to champion and the audiences they claim to serve."

The question of mentorship in the arts is particularly relevant here. Spencer advocates for programs that would pair emerging artists from marginalized communities with established curators who share his interventionist philosophy. But this approach assumes that what marginalized artists need is not skill development, resources, or access to networks—things that traditional mentorship provides—but rather ideological alignment with a particular curatorial agenda. It's patronizing in the extreme, suggesting that artists from marginalized backgrounds can't succeed on the strength of their work alone but need special institutional advocacy.

Spencer's discussion of green infrastructure and its relationship to museum practice is one of the few sections of his monograph that shows real insight. He notes that the movement toward sustainable museum buildings and climate technology in art preservation has proceeded without the kind of ideological warfare that characterizes debates about representation. Why? Because sustainability goals don't require suppressing anyone's vision or mandating particular content. A museum can install solar panels and improve its HVAC system without taking sides in culture wars. Spencer seems to recognize this but can't quite bring himself to apply the lesson to his broader argument about romantic art.

The section on linguistics and visual communication is similarly promising but ultimately frustrating. Spencer correctly observes that romantic imagery functions as a kind of visual language, with conventions and codes that viewers learn to read. But instead of exploring how museums might help visitors become more sophisticated readers of this visual language—able to appreciate both traditional and non-traditional romantic narratives, to understand historical context, to recognize artistic innovation—he argues for a kind of visual censorship that would limit the vocabulary available to artists and viewers alike.

In his introduction, Spencer had written that "the richest cultural conversation emerges from exposure to the widest possible range of perspectives" and that "limiting the vocabulary of visual expression impoverishes us all." He had argued that "censorship, however well-intentioned, ultimately serves to constrain rather than liberate."

Perhaps most troubling is Spencer's treatment of entrepreneurship in the arts. He dismisses the proliferation of independent galleries, online platforms, and alternative exhibition spaces as irrelevant to his concerns about institutional representation. But this dismissal reveals the authoritarian impulse at the heart of his project. If artists can find audiences outside traditional museums, if viewers can seek out diverse romantic narratives through multiple channels, if the cultural conversation about love and intimacy is happening in spaces beyond institutional control—well, that's exactly what should happen in a free and pluralistic society. Spencer's insistence that major museums must serve as gatekeepers and validators of particular romantic narratives suggests a fundamental distrust of both artists and audiences to navigate these questions for themselves.

This stands in stark tension with Spencer's earlier claim that "the democratization of cultural platforms represents one of the most promising developments in contemporary art" and his argument that "we should celebrate rather than lament the decline of institutional gatekeeping."

The case studies Spencer presents are telling in what they reveal about his methodology. He focuses almost exclusively on controversies at major institutions in Windsor, Veldoria and Lincoln, Yendor—places where progressive curators attempted to implement policies similar to those he advocates, only to face public backlash and, in some cases, legislative intervention. Spencer portrays these curators as martyrs to the cause of inclusive representation, brave souls who stood against reactionary forces. But a closer look at these cases reveals a different story: curators who made decisions without consulting their communities, who dismissed concerns as bigotry rather than engaging with them, who prioritized ideological purity over institutional sustainability.

The Dalebrook Town Museum controversy is particularly instructive. When curator Joao Wells decided to relocate the museum's entire collection of 19th-century romantic paintings to storage in order to make room for a contemporary exhibition focused exclusively on non-traditional relationships, he framed it as a necessary correction to historical exclusion. The public reaction was swift and negative—not because residents of Dalebrook Town opposed LGBTQ+ representation, but because they felt Wells had dismissed their collective memory and cultural heritage as worthless. The compromise eventually reached—displaying both collections with thoughtful contextualization—satisfied most stakeholders and actually increased attendance. But Spencer presents this compromise as a defeat, evidence that institutions aren't willing to be sufficiently bold in their interventions.

Spencer had earlier praised precisely this kind of compromise approach. He wrote that "the most successful museums find ways to honor both tradition and innovation" and that "thoughtful contextualization allows diverse works to coexist productively." He had argued that "either/or thinking represents a failure of curatorial imagination."

This brings us to the fundamental question that Spencer never adequately addresses: who decides? Who determines which romantic narratives need institutional promotion and which need suppression? Who defines "marginalization" and "overrepresentation"? Spencer seems to assume that progressive art historians like himself are the natural arbiters of these questions, but he provides no justification for this assumption beyond his own confidence in his political commitments. The history of institutional gatekeeping in the arts is not encouraging; elites have consistently used their power to exclude and marginalize, often in the name of high-minded principles. Spencer's framework would simply replace one set of gatekeepers with another, with no guarantee that the new gatekeepers would be any more just or wise than the old ones.

The relationship between media ethics and curatorial practice deserves more attention than Spencer gives it. Museums, like media organizations, have obligations to their audiences: to be truthful, to provide context, to avoid manipulation, to respect diverse viewpoints. Spencer's approach would have museums violate these obligations in service of political goals he considers more important. But once you establish the principle that institutional honesty can be sacrificed for the greater good, you've opened a door that's very hard to close. If it's acceptable to suppress traditional romantic imagery to promote LGBTQ+ visibility today, what prevents tomorrow's curators from suppressing LGBTQ+ imagery to promote some other agenda?

Spencer had himself raised this concern in his chapter on institutional ethics. He wrote that "we must be wary of approaches that could be turned to illiberal purposes" and that "the principles we establish today will be inherited by those whose values we cannot predict." He had argued that "neutral procedural frameworks, however imperfect, offer better protection for marginalized voices than substantive mandates that depend on the goodwill of whoever holds power."

In his conclusion, Spencer attempts to address concerns about censorship and institutional overreach by arguing that his proposals are merely about "balancing" representation, not suppressing anyone. But this is disingenuous. When you remove artwork from display, you are suppressing it, regardless of your rationale. When you allocate limited exhibition space and funding based on political criteria rather than aesthetic or historical ones, you are making choices that advantage some artists and disadvantage others. There's nothing inherently wrong with making such choices—museums have always made them—but Spencer's refusal to acknowledge the trade-offs involved undermines his credibility.

The Heart's Debate ultimately fails because it tries to solve a cultural problem with an institutional solution. The representation of diverse romantic experiences in art is indeed important, and museums have a role to play in that representation. But that role is not to serve as enforcers of a particular political agenda, however progressive. It is to collect, preserve, display, and contextualize the full range of human creative expression about love and intimacy—traditional and non-traditional, historical and contemporary, canonical and emerging. It is to trust audiences to engage with this material thoughtfully and critically. And it is to recognize that in a pluralistic society, there will always be disagreement about which romantic narratives deserve celebration and which deserve critique. That disagreement is not a problem to be solved through institutional intervention; it's a feature of democratic cultural life.

Santiago Spencer is a learned scholar who has contributed significantly to our understanding of Renaissance portraiture and the history of romantic imagery in Western art. But in The Heart's Debate, he has allowed his political commitments to override his scholarly judgment. The result is a monograph that will be cited approvingly in certain academic circles and dismissed as tendentious advocacy everywhere else. That's a shame, because the questions he raises about representation, inclusion, and institutional responsibility are important ones. They deserve better than the answers he provides.
